proposals.name: Sustained interior consciousness
proposals.instruction: Score high if the narration sustains a distinctive interior perspective -- the narrator's private reasoning, rationalizations, emotional drift, or perceptual filter is dramatized across the piece, not just reported as plot beats. Score low if the story is a sequence of external events with little or no access to a character's ongoing inner life, or if interiority appears only as a single stated emotion word.
proposals.rationale: R01's serial-killer narrator sustains self-justifying interior logic across five separate murders ('I vowed to protect...'); R11's narrator interrogates her own motives at length ('I'm not selfless... I felt so very important'). Comparable pieces like R13 and R37 are almost entirely external banter with no interior access.

proposals.name: Show-don't-tell characterization
proposals.instruction: High: character traits, intelligence, danger, or feeling are conveyed through concrete action, word choice, or behavior the reader must infer. Low: the narrator directly asserts a character's qualities in summary ('he seemed X, yet Y') or explains a character's motive/history in exposition rather than dramatizing it.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R22 reveal character entirely through physical action (wrestling a dragon into submission, marveling at gore) with no summary labeling. By contrast R15 states outright 'He seemed cold and intelligent, yet sad and dutiful,' and R31 tells us 'the man was a genius' via narrator summary rather than dramatizing the manipulation.

proposals.name: Causally escalating stakes (rising action)
proposals.instruction: High: each event in the story increases pressure or stakes and follows causally or emotionally from what preceded, building toward a climax. Low: events form an episodic list or chain reported after the fact, connected by 'and then' rather than by rising consequence.
proposals.rationale: R01 escalates from an accidental killing to a deliberate pattern of murders keyed to Emily's romantic life, each raising the stakes; R09 escalates through three successive 'gifts' of increasing cosmic scale. By contrast R21 reports a chain of classroom chaos as a flat list of mishaps recounted after the fact to a principal, with no rising tension of its own.

proposals.name: Payoff proportionate to setup
proposals.instruction: High: given how much setup or investment the story asks of the reader, the ending delivers proportionate closure, insight, reversal, or consequence. Low: the piece invests significant setup then trails off, under-resolves, or resolves with a payoff far thinner than the buildup warranted.
proposals.rationale: R04 invests in sensory buildup (the demon, the Clorox 'peacemaker') and pays it off with both confrontation and a warm coda; R06 pays off its 'sixteen generations' framing with a full-circle final line. By contrast R33 invests heavily in mysterious worldbuilding (Hextech, Cassandra's inhuman strength) but cuts off on an unresolved cliffhanger with a promotional sign-off substituting for closure.

proposals.name: Productive restraint / ambiguity
proposals.instruction: High: the story withholds explanation at a key moment and that withholding deepens meaning or productively unsettles the reader. Low: the story spells out its own logic or punchline in full, leaving nothing for the reader to complete, or any ambiguity present reads as unintentional confusion rather than a considered choice.
proposals.rationale: R03 ends on the unexplained, understated 'Maybe I didn't deserve to,' and R30 never resolves whether the coma or the dream-world is the real one. By contrast R37 fully explains its own joke's mechanics line by line ('An animal that possesses body features...'), leaving no ambiguity or work for the reader.

proposals.name: Prompt stakes taken seriously, not just a gag vehicle
proposals.instruction: High: the story engages with the emotional or moral weight implied by the prompt as real stakes for the characters. Low: the prompt's implied gravity (death, violence, loss) is used chiefly as raw material for a joke or ironic juxtaposition, with no character treating it as consequential.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R09 treat their premises (vigilante murder, species-altering first contact) as carrying genuine moral and emotional weight for the characters. By contrast R14 stages a sister learning both parents just died purely as a vehicle for a joke about teenage texting inanity, and R37 treats its premise as pure gag with no stakes.

proposals.name: Elaboration beyond the inciting gimmick
proposals.instruction: High: the story develops texture, consequence, or a secondary layer beyond the single joke or concept that launched it. Low: once the premise or joke is stated, the rest of the piece merely restates or extends the same beat without adding a new dimension (emotional, thematic, or plot).
proposals.rationale: R08 starts as a 'clumsy cadet with a weird dragon' joke but adds real vulnerability and family shame beneath the comedy; R22 layers humor, romantic tension, and desensitization-to-violence onto its isekai premise. By contrast R13 and R20 stay entirely within their opening joke (grumpy horse-curse banter; bureaucratic aliens) without adding a further layer.

proposals.name: Formal/structural risk that serves the content
proposals.instruction: High: the story takes a deliberate risk with form (a found document, an in-universe official register, a dialogue-only scene, verse-like line breaks) and that form does real work for the content. Low: the story uses a default straightforward scene-then-ending shape with no formal experimentation.
proposals.rationale: R25 is written as an in-universe scholarly survival-guide excerpt, letting it deliver worldbuilding with ironic distance; R28 is told entirely through Socratic dialogue that mirrors its quantum-theory subject; R12 uses minimalist line-broken prose to enact numbness. Compare the conventional scene-plus-punchline shape of R16 or R29, which take no formal risk.

proposals.name: Invented specificity / worldbuilding texture
proposals.instruction: High: the story contains particular, invented details (names, customs, turns of phrase, institutions) specific to its world rather than generic genre furniture. Low: the setting is described only in generic terms interchangeable with any story in the genre.
proposals.rationale: R02 invents 'the War of Too Many Uncles,' the peasant poet Alric Turnip, and the 'House of Many Mirrors' -- texture unique to its world; R25 invents the Gharchz, the Echlmaar'ch, and named star systems. By contrast R37's cosmology (unnamed God, generic animals, unnamed realm) and R13's fantasy trappings stay generic and interchangeable.

proposals.name: Concrete sensory/physical grounding
proposals.instruction: High: the story renders action through specific bodily sensation, sound, or physical detail (what a character feels, hears, touches) rather than abstract summary of what happened. Low: events are reported at a summary level ('X happened, then Y happened') without physical texture.
proposals.rationale: R06 grounds the dragon-taming in tactile specifics (harness sliding over a wet-slick face, weight crushing into hot sand); R38 renders taste and bodily horror concretely. By contrast R21's classroom chaos and R27's backstory are relayed through secondhand dialogue summary rather than physically rendered scenes.

proposals.name: Prose rhythm/control independent of surface correctness
proposals.instruction: Judge sentence-level rhythm and word choice on their own terms, separately from spelling or grammar errors: does the language's cadence and diction actively serve mood, urgency, or voice (high), or is it flat and serviceable regardless of correctness (low)? A grammatically clean but flavorless sentence should score lower than a grammatically rough sentence that is doing real expressive work.
proposals.rationale: R01 has grammar slips ('he as drunk') but a breathless, run-on cadence that enacts the narrator's casual relationship to danger; R39 has typos ('aliean,' 'exestential') but sustains a genuinely propulsive, ambitious sweep of ideas. Judge these on rhythm and voice, not correctness, versus flatly correct but inert prose like R26's plain declaratives.

proposals.name: Dialogue that carries subtext or characterization
proposals.instruction: High: dialogue exchanges imply more than they state, revealing character, tension, or relationship dynamics beyond moving the plot or delivering a punchline. Low: dialogue exists mainly to deliver exposition, set up a joke, or state information directly with no subtextual layer.
proposals.rationale: R28's Socratic back-and-forth reveals the student's unusual intelligence through the shape of his questions rather than any statement of intelligence; R32's negotiation scene reveals danger and backstory through what is and isn't said about the daughter's condition. By contrast R27's dialogue is built around a repeated name-mixup gag with no subtextual charge, and R37's dialogue exists purely to state and then explain the joke.

proposals.name: Narrative self-sufficiency from outside continuity/IP
proposals.instruction: High: the story is fully comprehensible and complete using only the prompt and the text given, without needing knowledge of another work, franchise, or prior installment. Low: understanding or fully appreciating the story depends on recognizing an external property, a shared fictional universe, or a previous post the reader has not been given.
proposals.rationale: R15 depends on recognizing both Game of Thrones' Joffrey and No Country for Old Men's Anton Chigurh to land its final beat; R31 is an alternate ending to the TV series The Night Manager and assumes familiarity with its plot and characters; R40 explicitly states 'This will make more sense if you read part 1 first.' Compare self-contained pieces like R01 or R06, which require nothing beyond the text given.

proposals.name: Paratextual intrusion into the fictional frame
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which sign-offs, subreddit plugs, or embedded hyperlinks to other posts interrupt or dilute the story's fictional frame. High (good) = no such intrusion, or it is cleanly separated after a clear ending. Low = promotional material or link-heavy continuity references are woven into the body of the narrative itself, breaking immersion mid-story.
proposals.rationale: R23 embeds multiple hyperlinks to other subreddit posts directly inside its narrative prose (e.g., 'the nanos Dara got from the goblins' linked mid-sentence), constantly breaking the fictional frame. R16 and R30 append word-count and subreddit-plug notes immediately after the emotional close. Compare R01, R06, or R09, which contain no such intrusion at all.

proposals.name: Fulfillment of the basic narrative contract
proposals.instruction: High: the piece is an actual worked story -- it has a scene, character(s), or a developed narrative idea responding to the prompt. Low: the piece is administrative, meta, or announcement text (e.g., a moderator post, a contest-results notice) that does not attempt a story at all, regardless of how well-written it is.
proposals.rationale: R17 is a moderator's contest-announcement post ('Well done everyone... Survivors will be reassigned to Antarctica') with no character or scene; R35 is an administrative explanation of a recurring subreddit feature, not a dramatized response to its own Russian-roulette prompt. Neither attempts fiction in response to the prompt the way every other row in this slice does.

proposals.name: Interiority: a specific mind with private, non-obvious content
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the piece is occupied by a particular consciousness reporting things only that consciousness would know or admit. Clearly satisfying: the narration carries mental content that cannot be deduced from the events themselves - a private shameful hope, a rationalization, an inconvenient preference, an association the character would never say aloud - and that content is specific to this character rather than generic. Clearly failing: the piece is a sequence of external events and speech acts with feelings named only in stock terms (he was terrified, rage filled her), or the point-of-view figure could be replaced by any competent stranger without a single sentence changing. A third-person story can score high if it renders a particular mind; a first-person story scores low if the 'I' is only a camera.
proposals.rationale: This is the sharpest split in the slice. R19 (dense .935 / card .019-class) has no scene at all and is nothing but a mind conceding that its own generosity was a power high; R24 (dense .986 / card .059) is entirely a dampened interior report, and the flatness is the content; R29 hides the narrator's secret wish that the egg has died. Against these, R01 (dense .148 / card .985) and R30 (dense .142 / card .930) are clean, well-staged scenes whose viewpoint figures have no mental content the plot does not already supply. A scorecard built around scene, dialogue and event has no cell for the thing R19 and R24 consist of.

proposals.name: Declines the easy moral verdict; narrator implicated
proposals.instruction: Score whether the text makes the reader hold two incompatible attitudes toward the same figure and refuses to settle them. Clearly satisfying: the sympathetic figure does something ugly, or the designated monster is given a real reason, and the piece does not step in to adjudicate; the narrator's own account quietly indicts the narrator. Clearly failing: a plainly designated villain receives a plainly deserved outcome, the narrator's virtue is never in question, or an out-group exists only to be laughed at or punished. Judge the story's stance, not the amount of violence.
proposals.rationale: R08 (dense .986 / card .149) has a narrator who cannot believe the official story that the aliens attacked first, says he is a military man who is paid not to ask questions, and ends by becoming the thing he killed; R37 (dense .939 / card .149) narrates escalating murder in the register of loyal friendship and never once notices; R31 and R11 both sit on unflattering feelings toward the person the narrator depends on or failed. Against these, R23 (dense .108 / card .967) imports a bad Joffrey and shoots him, and R32 (dense .108 / card .966) reduces its target to a punchline. Both of the latter are tidy and legible, which is exactly what a criterion bank rewards.

proposals.name: Emotional payoff produced by inference, not announced
proposals.instruction: Locate the piece's main emotional beat and ask how the reader receives it. Clearly satisfying: it arrives through an action, an image or a withheld reaction that the reader must convert into feeling, and the feeling word is never used. Clearly failing: the text names the feeling and then supplies the reassurance on schedule - a hug, a thank-you, a faint smile, a calm deep breath - so that the emotional content is delivered rather than constructed. This is about the payoff moment specifically, not about interiority in general; a story can be rich in interiority and still hand its ending over pre-digested.
proposals.rationale: R11 (dense .861 / card .050) never names grief: the burnt wedding photo slips from her fingers, black ash on green grass, and the refrain 'I was too late to stop it' does the rest; R40 (dense .899 / card .103) conveys attachment through a bleeding hand and a purr that sounds like a wounded animal. R06 (dense .020 / card .971) is the clean inverse - genuinely skilled sentence to sentence, but its close stacks thank you, a faint smile, and a calm deep breath, spelling out the comfort it has already staged; R15 (dense .090 / card .942) does the same with its toast. Explicit emotional resolution is easy for a criterion judge to confirm and is precisely what the dense model appears to discount.

proposals.name: Detail earns its place: load-bearing specificity, calibrated figuration
proposals.instruction: Two-part composite; score low if either half fails badly. (i) Do the concrete nouns change what the reader can infer or do - position, capability, threat, class, history, mechanics of the action - or are they an inventory that could be deleted with no loss? (ii) Is the figurative pitch proportional to the stakes of the moment being described? Clearly satisfying: description that is also the mechanics of what is happening, with metaphor reserved for moments that carry weight. Clearly failing: a paragraph cataloguing furniture colours, screen sizes and appliance brands; or an ordinary domestic beat narrated at operatic pitch.
proposals.rationale: R35 (dense .131 / card .953) spends two full paragraphs itemising carpet, dresser, desk, a 32 inch flat screen and an Apple TV, none of which does anything; R06 (dense .020 / card .971) renders a child's nightmare with 'rage ensnares Angie in its thorny coils' and 'Clorox peacemaker'; R12 (dense .189 / card .982) gives its teenager hair falling 'in a waterfall down her back'. Against these, R29 (dense .947 / card .066) builds every image out of working parts - harness, traces, wet-slick membrane, hot sand - and R13 (dense .954 / card .170) builds dread from a mouse swinging on its cord. A bank with a vivid-description criterion cannot tell inventory and inflation apart from work.

proposals.name: Sentence-level freshness; low stock-phrase density
proposals.instruction: Sample the narration and count the formulations that arrive pre-assembled: heart pounding in his throat, now or never, a chill ran down her spine, wiped the sweat from his brow, snapped back, said calmly, prayed for luck. Clearly satisfying: few or none, and the syntax has a rhythm of its own rather than a default cadence. Clearly failing: the prose is largely built from such units, so that a reader can complete most sentences from their openings. Do not penalise spelling or grammatical error under this criterion - penalise only second-hand phrasing.
proposals.rationale: R12 (dense .189 / card .982) uses heart pounding twice in four paragraphs plus 'Now or never' and 'prayed for luck to any gods who might be listening'; R25 (dense .886 / card .059) opens with wiped the sweat from his brow and a chill of recognition down the spine - and is the one row where this failure coexists with real strengths, which is informative. Against these, R26 (dense .924 / card .112) invents 'the War of Too Many Uncles' and commoners with 'pleasant elbows', and R17 (dense .972 / card .170) sustains a coined bureaucratic idiom. A bank that checks for imagery and mechanics scores fluent cliche as correct prose.

proposals.name: At least one invented rule or institution drives the scene
proposals.instruction: Ask whether the piece contains a specific practice, economy, law, procedure or custom that is not standard issue for its genre, and whether the scene actually turns on it. Clearly satisfying: an invented rule with consequences, such that removing it would collapse the scene. Clearly failing: the setting is assembled entirely from off-the-shelf furniture - tavern, hooded bandit, witch's curse, ominous mage upstairs, magic healing stream - and the invented material is limited to proper nouns. Judge invention, not exoticism: an invented rule can be mundane.
proposals.rationale: R17 (dense .972 / card .170) is built on 'first exposure-first extinction' and pays it off with an interstellar conference deciding to go quiet; R29 (dense .947 / card .066) turns on a guild rule against helping hatchlings out of the shell that is enforced by hatchlings eating initiates; R26 turns on the termination fee. Against these, R04 (dense .067 / card .932) is dwarf, witch's curse, magic stream, and R12 (dense .189 / card .982) is tavern, ogre-blooded bouncer, mysterious patron - both immaculately competent and both inventing nothing. Prompt-adherence and coherent-worldbuilding criteria mark genre defaults as passes.

proposals.name: No mutual-knowledge exposition; information arrives under pressure
proposals.instruction: Score how the reader learns what the world is. Clearly satisfying: facts reach the reader because a character needs them, uses them, is hurt by them, or acts on them, and any background is inferable from behaviour. Clearly failing: characters recite to one another facts that both plainly already possess - a policy 'the Ensemble put in place over a century ago', a house rule that the speaker and listener have both lived under for decades - or the narration halts to brief the reader on history it could have shown.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense .148 / card .985) has Regalis and Typhon rehearse the Treaty of Silence and the Ensemble's century-old policy at each other, and R10 (dense .101 / card .922) has Randy explain the haunted house's business model and rules to a resident ghost. Both read as fully populated scenes with conflict, dialogue and a twist, which is why a criterion bank ranks them near the top. Against these, R29 conveys the guild's entire rule set by having hatchlings eat two initiates on the page, and R08 reconstructs its mission sideways through what the narrator cannot stop replaying.

proposals.name: Speaker-distinct dialogue: lines cannot be reassigned
proposals.instruction: Take two speakers and test whether their lines could be swapped without the reader noticing. Clearly satisfying: idiom, register, agenda and rhythm differ enough that attributions would be recoverable with all tags removed. Clearly failing: the speakers are one voice split in two, holding positions rather than having manners; or an unattributed exchange in which the reader loses track of who is talking. Score the differentiation, not the wit.
proposals.rationale: R36 (dense .158 / card .951) runs an entire unattributed exchange in which Dexter, his companion and God are mutually indistinguishable; R32 (dense .108 / card .966) gives Vlommik and Qreclops one shared voice; R01's two whales differ only in policy position. Against these, R28 (dense .945 / card .030) is nothing but bracket tags and is never for a second ambiguous, because the professor's classroom patter and the student's dogged narrowing are different instruments; R27 sets Eugene's showman patter against Devin's schedule-keeping. Dialogue-presence and dialogue-naturalness criteria both pass R36 and R32.

proposals.name: Self-sufficient: no prior installment, source work or link required
proposals.instruction: Ask whether a reader holding only the writing prompt and this text can follow it. Clearly satisfying: every person, relationship and prior event the story leans on is supplied inside the piece. Clearly failing: the story depends on a named source work, an earlier installment, or linked posts to be intelligible - proper nouns and grievances arrive already-loaded, or the text explicitly directs the reader to read something else first. Borrowing a widely known public character is not automatically a failure if the piece supplies what it needs; inheriting a private cast is.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense .078 / card .915) drops Roper, Corky, Pine, Jed, Burr and Danny plus 'the lobster incident' and 'that grand finale on the ship' with no orientation at all; R18 (dense .056 / card .953) opens by telling the reader to read part one first; R21 (dense .027 / card .814) threads five inline links to previous stories through its dialogue. All three read as confident and detailed at the sentence level, which is what a scorecard can see; none is legible on its own terms. R17 and R29 by contrast hand the reader everything required.

proposals.name: Premise metabolized, not narrated
proposals.instruction: Score whether the prompt functions as a starting condition or as the payload. Clearly satisfying: the premise is granted early and the length is spent on what follows from it - a consequence, a complication, a cost the premise implies but does not state. Clearly failing: the piece's whole content is restatement or literal execution of the prompt - it describes the premise, narrates its own composition, or stages exactly the scene the prompt already described and stops. Note that adherence and non-adherence are both irrelevant here: a story can follow the prompt closely and still push far past it.
proposals.rationale: R05 (dense .020 / card .961) narrates reading the prompt and deciding to write, and states outright that it has no substance; R39 (dense .126 / card .980) performs the prompt's literal instruction and appends an authorial note about emoji. Both are maximally on-prompt, which any prompt-fidelity criterion rewards. Against these, R08 (dense .986 / card .149) buries the prompt's line about human mouths as a late throwaway inside a much larger account of contamination, and R19 (dense .935) converts a level-3008 gimmick into a confession about the pleasure of being needed.

proposals.name: The middle develops: escalation or a conceptual second move
proposals.instruction: Judging only the shown text and not penalising a marked middle omission, ask whether each successive beat raises the stakes, changes the situation, or extends the idea into an implication absent from the opening beat. Clearly satisfying: later beats could not be moved earlier without breaking the piece. Clearly failing: the piece states its idea and then repeats, ornaments or re-jokes it, ending in the same conceptual place it began.
proposals.rationale: R02 (dense .889 / card .072) is almost pure escalation - abducted, dismembered, self-reassembled, sniped, reassembled, obliterated - and its ratchet is the craft; R09 (dense .895 / card .117) moves through three gifts, each enlarging the scale until the species is speaking in scripture; R17 goes rule, precedent case, Terran anomaly, galactic policy. Against these, R36 (dense .158 / card .951) tells one platypus joke and stops, R27 (dense .167 / card .967) restates a single let-me-finish-my-monologue joke three times, and R22 holds one tone for its full length.

proposals.name: Ending changes the meaning of what preceded
proposals.instruction: Score the final beat by what it does to the earlier text. Clearly satisfying: it forces a re-reading - it reveals what the narrator has become, converts a victory into a cost, or leaves a pressure the reader now has to hold. Clearly failing: it caps and dissolves the situation, so nothing earlier is altered. A quiet ending can score high, and a twist can score low if it changes only the plot and not how the preceding text reads.
proposals.rationale: R08 (dense .986 / card .149) ends on a date with writhing movements and an unhinging jaw, which retroactively converts 'I am not sure why I said that to the creature' into a symptom; R16 (dense .943 / card .030) wins the case and is struck mute, turning acquittal into sentence; R33 (dense .918 / card .127) has the parents split and merge, turning coma-comedy into captivity. Against these, R04 (dense .067 / card .932) closes 'ready to commit more misadventures', R22 (dense .147 / card .964) hacks the clock and clocks out, and R15 goes to the pub. A twist-present or resolution-present criterion cannot separate the two columns.

proposals.name: Something irreversible is spent
proposals.instruction: Ask what the piece has permanently removed by its last line - a life, a capability, a trust, a relationship, an option - and whether it stays removed. Clearly satisfying: a loss the story does not undo, take back, or make comic-safe. Clearly failing: the situation is fully recoverable, is restored within the piece, or is staged so that risk is retrospectively absent. Comic pieces can score high, because a cost can be funny; violent pieces can score low, because carnage without consequence costs nothing.
proposals.rationale: R11 (dense .861 / card .050) ends with her dead and the narrator having stopped telling stories at all; R29 (dense .947 / card .066) eats two initiates on the page and takes away the narrator's private hope of a reprieve; R16 removes a species' speech. Against these, R04 (dense .067 / card .932) cures the curse and walks home, R10 (dense .101 / card .922) parks Lukas comically in a portrait, and R15 (dense .090 / card .942) fully reconstitutes the corpse and buys it a drink. Stakes-present criteria register threat, not expenditure, and all three low rows stage plenty of threat.

proposals.name: Distinctive narrating idiom, scored with mechanics disregarded
proposals.instruction: Deliberately set aside spelling, grammar, punctuation, typography, second-language constructions and formatting. Ask only whether the narration has a consistent, particular idiom - diction, rhythm, a characteristic move - that could not be swapped for another narrator's, and whether it holds for the whole piece. Clearly satisfying: a voice you could pick out of a lineup, maintained end to end. Clearly failing: neutral correct prose with no fingerprint, or a voice that starts distinctive and quietly reverts to default narration. Do not reward roughness; simply do not let it decide the score.
proposals.rationale: This is a direct correction for what the scorecard appears to over-weight. R14 (dense .846 / card .024) is misspelled throughout - alieans, habital, ceentury, preverbial - yet sustains a specific mock-lecture debunking voice; R33 (dense .918 / card .127) is lowercase and comma-spliced but its drowsy petulant register is unmistakable; R34 (dense .921 / card .144) carries typos and an apology for non-native English while marching from Caesar to Da Vinci to Wozniak to a ringing telephone. Against these, R30 (dense .142 / card .930) and R25 are clean, correct and anonymous. Mechanics are trivially scoreable by a criterion judge; idiom is not.

proposals.name: Form enacts content and outlives the formal gag
proposals.instruction: Two-part composite; both halves required for a high score. (i) Does the chosen form - in-world document, transcript, chat log, fragmented lines, mock essay, second-person address - represent something about the material, rather than being arbitrary layout? (ii) Once the formal conceit has been understood, does the piece still deliver something further: an event, an implication, a turn? Clearly satisfying: both. Clearly failing: an ordinary story wearing an arbitrary costume, or a form that constitutes the entire content, so that a reader who grasps the conceit in the first few lines has already received everything the piece will give.
proposals.rationale: R24 (dense .986 / card .059) breaks into short trailing fragments that enact the numbed affect they describe, and still arrives at extinction-by-apathy; R17 (dense .972 / card .170) sustains an in-world containment protocol without one break in register and pays it off with policy; R28 (dense .945 / card .030) is a bare bracket-tagged transcript that nevertheless lands a real objection to the thought experiment. Against these, R39 (dense .126 / card .980) is a chat log whose form is the whole joke, and appends a parenthesis explaining it, and R05 (dense .020 / card .961) is a formal conceit that concedes it has nothing behind it. Non-standard formatting is exactly the sort of thing a prose-quality bank scores as a defect in one direction or a novelty in the other, never as work being done.

proposals.name: Prompt-to-premise transformation
proposals.instruction: Score how fully the story turns the prompt into a premise that generates meaningful events. High scores use the prompt to create consequences, conflict, or world logic; low scores merely restate it, append a generic gag, or barely use it.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, and R36 develop their prompts into broader systems with consequences, whereas R27 and R28 mostly repeat or discuss the assignment.

proposals.name: Setup-to-payoff causality
proposals.instruction: Score whether early details later become causally or thematically important. High scores make setup alter the ending or a later decision; low scores leave details ornamental or make the payoff feel arbitrary.
proposals.rationale: R20, R34, and R40 plant physical or behavioral details that matter later; R08 and R17 offer premises whose details do not produce a comparably earned payoff.

proposals.name: Layered character motivation
proposals.instruction: Score whether characters act from multiple, conflicting motives that the text makes legible. High scores show desire, fear, loyalty, resentment, or self-interest operating together; low scores give characters only a single obvious trait or function.
proposals.rationale: R06, R22, and R30 make generosity, guilt, dependence, and resentment coexist; R08 and R17 rely mainly on characters delivering the premise.

proposals.name: Moral complication
proposals.instruction: Score whether the story complicates the reader’s moral judgment rather than announcing an easy good-versus-evil position. High scores expose hypocrisy, unintended harm, or defensible motives behind troubling behavior; low scores leave ethical conclusions obvious and unexamined.
proposals.rationale: R06, R20, and R33 make apparently good or bad actions morally unstable, while R25 and R35 resolve their ethical material through comparatively simple judgments.

proposals.name: Distinctive character voice
proposals.instruction: Score how clearly diction, rhythm, dialogue, and narration distinguish the characters and remain consistent with them. High scores make speakers identifiable without tags; low scores make everyone sound interchangeable or communicate mainly through exposition.
proposals.rationale: R18, R29, and R36 use strongly differentiated voices to carry comedy and characterization; R08 and R17 have dialogue that mainly states information or the joke.

proposals.name: Implicit worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score whether the world emerges through specific institutions, customs, history, and consequences embedded in the action. High scores let readers infer a coherent society without stopping for an encyclopedia; low scores supply arbitrary labels or detached exposition without lived implications.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, and R29 imply large social systems through concrete practices and historical consequences; R25 and R37 explain speculative systems more than they dramatize them.

proposals.name: Choice-driven escalation
proposals.instruction: Score whether each major beat creates a more difficult situation through a character’s choice or resistance. High scores build pressure toward an irreversible turn; low scores remain static, summarize events, or place disconnected incidents side by side.
proposals.rationale: R22, R34, and R38 escalate through decisions made under pressure; R19 and R27 contain little developing conflict beyond their initial premise.

proposals.name: Ending recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score whether the ending changes the meaning of what came before. High scores reveal a new identity, consequence, or interpretation that makes earlier details resonate differently; low scores stop at the first predictable explanation or punchline.
proposals.rationale: R20, R21, and R38 use final revelations or reversals to reinterpret earlier scenes; R10 and R27 end largely by confirming what the setup already established.

proposals.name: Functional sensory detail
proposals.instruction: Score whether concrete sensory and physical details do more than decorate the scene. High scores use texture, sound, smell, or bodily action to reveal danger, mood, setting, or character; low scores use generic description or clutter with no narrative function.
proposals.rationale: R11, R22, and R34 make rooms, bodies, and objects carry emotional or plot information; R17 and R25 rely more heavily on abstract explanation and generic scene description.

proposals.name: Motif-based cohesion
proposals.instruction: Score whether a repeated image, object, phrase, or sensory pattern develops across the story. High scores make the recurrence accumulate meaning; low scores introduce vivid images once without connecting them to the story’s central concern.
proposals.rationale: R20’s mouth and infection, R22’s photographs and listening, and R40’s camera clicks build thematic continuity; R08 and R17 use memorable concepts without comparable recurring structure.

proposals.name: Tonal control
proposals.instruction: Score whether shifts among humor, horror, sentiment, and seriousness feel deliberate and preserve the intended stakes. High scores make tonal contrasts reinforce the premise; low scores let jokes, meta commentary, or abrupt melodrama dissolve the scene’s emotional pressure.
proposals.rationale: R18, R31, and R34 sustain comic darkness while preserving stakes; R15 and R24 repeatedly interrupt their fiction with framing or authorial material that weakens tonal immersion.

proposals.name: Second-order premise consequences
proposals.instruction: Score whether the story follows its premise into an unexpected social, psychological, or technological consequence. High scores explore what the premise changes beyond the immediate gag; low scores deliver only the most obvious literal result.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, and R37 extrapolate speculative premises into civilization-scale consequences; R08 and R35 largely stop at a single surface-level joke or crossover encounter.

proposals.name: POV-shaped perception
proposals.instruction: Score whether the narrator’s mental state and limitations shape what is noticed, described, and misunderstood. High scores make perspective itself meaningful; low scores present events as neutral reporting or change viewpoint logic without purpose.
proposals.rationale: R09, R20, and R21 filter reality through numbness, infection, trauma, or delusion; R17 and R25 are comparatively detached summaries with little individualized perception.

proposals.name: Self-contained orientation
proposals.instruction: Score whether a reader can understand the characters, stakes, and relevant world rules from the supplied story alone. High scores provide necessary context economically; low scores depend on linked installments, outside lore, or unexplained framing material.
proposals.rationale: R15, R28, and R40 explicitly rely on prior posts, external links, or continuation context; R29 and R34 establish their unusual settings within the presented text.

proposals.name: Information-dense economy
proposals.instruction: Score how efficiently each sentence advances plot, character, atmosphere, or worldbuilding. High scores make most passages serve multiple functions; low scores repeat the premise, pad transitions, or explain information that could be dramatized.
proposals.rationale: R14, R29, and R36 combine exposition with voice, setting, and conflict; R17, R19, and R27 contain substantial material that advances little beyond the initial concept.

proposals.name: Psychological contradiction
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s motives, feelings, or self-image conflict in specific, credible ways; score low when characters have one plainly stated motive with no inner friction.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R31 derive force from narrators whose self-justifications conflict with their actions; R36 similarly complicates protective love with murderous obsession.

proposals.name: Premise consequences
proposals.instruction: Score high when the speculative premise produces concrete personal or societal consequences beyond its initial gimmick; score low when it remains mainly a backdrop or punchline.
proposals.rationale: R03 extrapolates infection into emotional and reproductive decline, while R18 develops a galactic doctrine around detectable civilizations; R37 extends alien technology across human history.

proposals.name: Sensory embodiment
proposals.instruction: Score high when setting, danger, or emotion is made tangible through precise sensory details and physical behavior; score low when events are described abstractly or generically.
proposals.rationale: R04 uses smoke, bile, ash, and sirens to embody trauma, while R12 grounds supernatural danger in smells, grime, heat, and bodily reactions; R28 makes hatching physical and perilous.

proposals.name: Causal escalation
proposals.instruction: Score high when each major beat logically worsens, complicates, or redirects the preceding problem toward a payoff; score low when incidents are merely appended or resolved without buildup.
proposals.rationale: R04 escalates from missed intervention to personal guilt, and R30 chains small accidents into a comic catastrophe; R34 establishes scarcity, threat, and mounting danger before confrontation.

proposals.name: Consequential agency
proposals.instruction: Score high when a protagonist makes difficult choices that materially change events and reveal character; score low when the protagonist mainly observes, receives explanations, or is carried by coincidence.
proposals.rationale: R16 centers Typhon’s deliberate rebellion, R28 makes the narrator actively control a dangerous hatchling, and R39 shows the arms dealer preparing and using an escape plan.

proposals.name: Recontextualizing ending
proposals.instruction: Score high when the ending meaningfully changes how earlier details are understood or completes a prepared implication; score low when it merely stops, repeats the premise, or adds an arbitrary final line.
proposals.rationale: R20’s final message reframes the apparent horror, R31’s later transformation reinterprets the bite, and R36’s wedding scene exposes the narrator’s continuing danger.

proposals.name: Controlled tonal contrast
proposals.instruction: Score high when shifts between comedy, horror, tenderness, or seriousness are deliberate and mutually illuminating; score low when tonal changes feel accidental, discordant, or purely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R05 combines urban disorientation with a tender reunion, R17 makes grotesque necromancy affectionate, and R35 uses comic banter to sustain a fantasy misadventure.

proposals.name: Distinctive narrative voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, rhythm, attitude, and omissions create a recognizable narrator or authorial persona suited to the story; score low when the prose sounds generic, interchangeable, or mechanically imitative.
proposals.rationale: R01’s confessional cynicism, R33’s ornate satirical voice, and R35’s irreverent fantasy banter each make the narration inseparable from the story’s identity.

proposals.name: Specific relationship dynamics
proposals.instruction: Score high when relationships are revealed through particular habits, tensions, histories, and reciprocal behavior; score low when characters are connected only by labels or plot functions.
proposals.rationale: R05 conveys attachment through 406’s search and Elise’s response, R12 builds sisterly protection through shared history, and R22 makes the cadet-dragon bond concrete through care and frustration.

proposals.name: Premise originality
proposals.instruction: Score high when the response discovers an uncommon angle, implication, or character consequence within the prompt; score low when it delivers the most predictable joke, crossover, or reversal available.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R11 rely heavily on their prompts’ immediate jokes, while R19 uses a familiar conspiracy gag; their contrast with stranger approaches in R16 and R33 motivates this criterion.

proposals.name: Dramatized conflict
proposals.instruction: Score high when the central problem unfolds through scenes, actions, and dialogue that force immediate choices; score low when the story mostly summarizes history, explains an idea, or presents an exchange without dramatized stakes.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R19 largely explain their worlds and premise, while R11 and R23 mainly stage an idea or joke; R04 and R17 show how active scenes create stronger dramatic evidence.

proposals.name: Narrative economy
proposals.instruction: Score high when nearly every included detail develops character, setting, tension, or payoff; score low when the piece contains digressions, promotional material, repetition, or ornamental information that does not advance the story.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R32 devote most of their text to framing or meta-commentary, and R40 compresses the premise into disconnected chat fragments; R04 and R28 demonstrate denser narrative use of detail.

proposals.name: Rules shown through action
proposals.instruction: Score high when unusual world rules are demonstrated through consequences, behavior, and conflicts rather than merely asserted; score low when the rules remain exposition with little effect on events.
proposals.rationale: R10 makes magical technical support operational through a caller’s problem, R16 dramatizes whale governance through confrontation, and R39 embeds its economic rules in a transaction and escape.

proposals.name: Ethical complexity
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story makes competing moral interpretations plausible without flattening them into a simple hero-villain judgment; score low when morality is announced as obvious or characters’ actions receive no meaningful tension.
proposals.rationale: R01 questions altruism and self-interest, R08 distinguishes cruelty from duty, and R31 complicates justified self-defense with fear, attraction, and possible infection.

proposals.name: Calibrated ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story withholds selected information that invites inference while preserving enough cues for coherent interpretation; score low when everything is overexplained or uncertainty results from missing logic and unclear sequencing.
proposals.rationale: R20 leaves the AI’s intentions to be inferred from its staged reveal, R24 destabilizes reality through shifting identities and repetition, and R31 uses an incomplete transformation to make interpretation part of the experience.
